title: Shortest Paths with Dijkstra
excerpt: BFS finds the fewest hops, which stops meaning the cheapest route the moment edges carry costs. Work out what you can safely commit to and Dijkstra's rule builds itself.

content.text: You already have an algorithm that finds shortest paths. Breadth-first search does it, and it does it perfectly on one condition: every edge has to cost the same to cross. Take that condition away and BFS quietly starts giving wrong answers.

Here is where it breaks. Suppose you are routing between towns and the roads have real lengths. One road runs straight from A to D and it is 100 kilometers long, while another route goes A to B to C to D, three roads of 10 kilometers each. BFS counts hops, so it reports the single 100 km road as the shortest path, because one is smaller than three. Anyone holding a map can see that 30 beats 100.

So the question this page answers is not really "what is Dijkstra's algorithm". It is this: once edges have costs, what do you actually know for certain at any given moment, and how little do you need to know before you can safely commit to an answer?

body.text: Start with the obvious idea, then watch it fail

content.text: The first thing most people try is the natural one. Stand at the source. Walk to whichever neighbor is nearest. From there, walk to whichever neighbor is nearest again, and keep going until you arrive. It feels sensible, it is easy to write, and it is wrong.
Take this graph. From A you can reach B for a cost of 1, or C for a cost of 4.

The nearest-neighbor walk goes to B first, because 1 is smaller than 4, and then has no choice but to pay 50 to reach D. Total: 51. The route through C costs 4 plus 1, which is 5. The greedy walk lost by a factor of ten, and it lost because it committed to B on the strength of one cheap edge, with no idea what lay behind it.
That is the useful part of the failure. A cheap first step tells you nothing about the total. So a correct algorithm cannot commit to a
route
. The question left over is whether there is anything at all it can safely commit to.

body.text: The one thing you can be certain about

content.text: Suppose you know the true distance from the source to a handful of nodes, and for every other node you have only a best guess: the cheapest route you have found so far, which might yet be beaten.
Now look at whichever guessed node has the
smallest
guess. Call it X, and say its guess is 12. The claim is that 12 is not a guess at all. It is the true shortest distance to X, and nothing you discover later can lower it.

The argument is worth walking through slowly, because once you believe it the rest of the algorithm falls out of it on its own. Imagine some cheaper route to X exists that you have not found yet. That route starts at the source and ends at X, so at some point it has to leave the set of nodes you already know for certain and step into the unknown. Call the first unknown node it touches Y.

Reaching Y already costs at least as much as Y's own current guess, because that guess is the cheapest known way in. And Y's guess cannot be smaller than X's, since you picked X as the smallest one. So the imagined route has already spent at least 12 by the time it reaches Y, and it still has the rest of the journey to X ahead of it. It cannot come in under 12.
One assumption is hiding in that last sentence, and the whole algorithm rests on it:
the rest of the journey cannot cost less than nothing

. If every edge costs zero or more, adding more road can never make a trip cheaper, so the imagined cheaper route is impossible and 12 is final. Hold on to that. It is precisely what negative edges take away, and we come back to it at the end.

body.text: The algorithm, now that you would have guessed it

content.text: Everything follows from that one certainty. If the smallest guess is always already correct, then you can turn guesses into facts one at a time, cheapest first, and never revisit a decision.

Give every node a best-known distance. The source gets 0, because standing still is free. Everything else gets infinity, which is just a way of writing "no route found yet". Then repeat two steps until you run out of nodes.
One.
Among the nodes you have not finalised, take the one with the smallest best-known distance and mark it settled. By the argument above, its number is now permanent.
Two.
Look at each of that node's neighbors and ask a single question: is going through this node cheaper than the best route I currently know to that neighbor? If it is, write down the smaller number.
That second step is called
relaxing
an edge, a piece of vocabulary considerably more intimidating than the idea behind it. Relaxing edge
u -> v
means checking whether
dist[u] + weight(u,v)
is less than
dist[v]
, and writing it down when it is. The name comes from picturing each distance as a stretched constraint that you let settle to a lower value once you find one.

Reading the two rules is not the same as believing them. Below is the graph every round in this section runs on, five nodes and six weighted edges. Click a node to try it yourself, or just read on: every number below is worked out by hand next.
Everything starts unknown except the source itself.
A has the smallest number, so A settles at 0. Relaxing its two edges gives B a route costing 2 and C a route costing 5.

The smallest unsettled number is now B at 2, so B settles. From B you can reach C for 2 plus 1, which is 3. That beats the 5 you had, so C drops to 3. You can also reach D for 2 plus 7, which is 9, and 9 beats infinity, so D becomes 9.

C is now the smallest unsettled node at 3, so it settles. From C you reach D for 3 plus 2, which is 5, and that beats the 9 you wrote a moment ago, so D improves to 5. This is the moment worth pausing on. D's value changed after it had already been discovered. Discovery and certainty are different things.
D settles at 5 and hands E a route of 5 plus 3, which is 8. Then E settles at 8 and there is nothing left to do.

Look back at D. It was 9, then 5, then final. Had you settled D the first time you saw a number for it, you would have shipped an answer nearly twice the true cost. The rule that saves you is not "settle a node when you reach it" but "settle a node when it is the cheapest thing left anywhere in the graph".

The number floating above each node is its best-known distance. Watch the numbers fall from infinity as better routes turn up, and watch the panel record which ones have been locked in. Try starting from a different node, and predict the first two settlements before you press play.

body.text: Getting the actual route, not just the number

content.text: So far the algorithm produces distances. Usually you want the road, not the mileage. The fix is small: whenever you improve a node's distance, also record which node you came from.

That single extra field gives you every shortest path at once. To read the route to E, start at E, jump to its recorded predecessor, and keep jumping until you land on the source, then reverse what you collected. The predecessors form a tree rooted at the source containing a shortest path to every reachable node, which is a lot of value for one array.

body.text: Where the running time comes from

content.text: It is worth deriving the cost rather than memorising it, because the derivation tells you which implementation to reach for.

Each of the V nodes settles exactly once, and settling means finding the smallest remaining number. Each of the E edges is relaxed once, when the node at its tail settles. So the total work is V smallest-finds plus E relaxations, and everything depends on how fast those two operations are.

The array version wins on dense graphs, where E approaches V squared and the scan cost is swamped anyway. The heap wins on sparse graphs, which covers most real road and network data. If you only ever remember one version, remember the heap.

One practical detail trips people up. Most heap implementations cannot cheaply lower a key that is already inside, so the usual trick is to push the improved entry and leave the stale one in place. When a stale entry surfaces later its distance no longer matches the node's current best, so you skip it. That is the
if (d > dist[u]) continue;
line in the code below. Without it the algorithm still terminates, but it repeats work it has already done.

Go back to the argument that made all of this work. It needed one thing: extra edges can never reduce a total. Allow a negative edge and that guarantee disappears, and the algorithm's correctness goes with it.
Here is the smallest example that shows it. Three nodes, three edges.

Dijkstra settles A at 0, then looks around and sees B at 2 and C at 3. B is smaller, so B settles at 2 and is never reconsidered. Only afterwards does C settle at 3 and reveal a route to B costing 3 plus -2, which is 1. The true answer for B is 1, the algorithm already committed to 2, and it has no mechanism for taking a settlement back.

Notice that this is not a bug in some edge case of the implementation. It is the proof itself failing, which is why the fix is a different algorithm rather than a patch. Bellman-Ford drops the idea of settling nodes in a fixed order and relaxes every edge repeatedly instead. That costs more, and it survives negative weights.

body.text: Mistakes worth knowing about in advance

content.text: Settling a node the moment you first reach it.

This is the most common error by a wide margin, and the trace above shows the damage: D was discovered at 9 and finished at 5. A node is only safe to settle once it is the cheapest unsettled node in the graph.
Running it on negative edges because the answer looked plausible.
Dijkstra does not crash on negative weights. It returns a confident wrong number, which is worse. Check the weights before you choose the algorithm.
Forgetting the stale-entry check with a heap.
Without the skip, old entries get processed again carrying distances that are no longer current. On large graphs that turns into a real slowdown.
Assuming unreachable means zero.
Nodes with no route from the source keep their infinity. Initialize with a value you can recognize afterwards, and never with 0.
Nothing here should surprise you now. The only line doing real thinking is the comparison inside the inner loop.

questions.prompt: Why is it safe to permanently settle the unsettled node with the smallest distance?

options.label: Any cheaper route would have to leave the settled set first, and that first step already costs at least as much
Because the graph is sorted by weight before the algorithm runs
Because every node is visited exactly once

questions.prompt: In the worked trace, D was assigned 9 and later changed to 5. What does that show?

options.label: Reaching a node is not the same as knowing its final distance
The graph contained a negative edge
The heap was missing its stale-entry check

questions.prompt: A graph has one edge of weight -2 and the rest are positive. What happens if you run Dijkstra?

options.label: It may return a wrong answer with no error, because a settled node is never revised
It works, since only negative cycles cause trouble

questions.prompt: What does relaxing edge u to v actually do?

options.label: Checks whether going through u beats v's best known distance, and updates it if so
Removes the edge once both endpoints are settled
Reduces the edge's weight so the search finishes sooner

seoTitle: Dijkstra's Algorithm Explained With a Worked Example
seoDescription: Dijkstra's algorithm derived step by step: why greedy nearest-neighbor fails, why settling the smallest tentative distance is provably safe, a full hand trace, and exactly where negative weights break the argument.
